series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] sched/numa: do not let the per-VMA PID filter gate promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) balancing mechanism, specifically related to VMA (Virtual Memory Area) scanning and promotion. The existing implementation prevents new scans from causing faults for potentially hours or days by filtering out VMAs that have not been hint-faulted. However, this leads to a situation where large shmem VMAs can hold the scan cursor for an extended period, causing other VMAs to be skipped due to 'inactivity'. The patch series introduces a new restricted scan mechanism that scans rejected VMAs and looks only at folios on non-toptier nodes, promoting candidates from the whole address space while maintaining top-tier marking unchanged.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses an issue in memory tiering where read-only file-backed mappings are not being scanned, leading to inefficient promotion of pages. The patch introduces a new function `vma_is_ro_file` to identify such mappings and modifies the `task_numa_work` function to scan these VMAs with the slow_only restriction. This ensures that only non-toptier folios are made hint-faultable, preventing unnecessary rescanning.

>  			if (!(sysctl_numa_balancing_mode &
>  			      NUMA_BALANCING_MEMORY_TIERING)) {

Sashiko thinks this causes unneeded rescanning, but I don't think it
does. The cursor prevents it from restarting, and when we loop back
around reset_ptenuma_scan() bumps the sequence.

It also had concerns about concurrent scanners and ptl lock contention,
but mm->numa_next_scan only admits one per scan period.

Either way on a rewalk the scan hits pte_protnone() and moves on.

~Gregory

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm/mempolicy: use SRCU for the weighted interleave state
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces the current implementation of weighted interleave state management in the Linux kernel's memory policy module with a new approach using SRCU (Schedulable RCU) to pin the global iw_table object and use it in-place. This change allows for more efficient handling of concurrent updates to the weights, reducing the need for synchronization and improving performance. The patch also introduces a new mechanism for retiring the weighted interleave state, which involves calling SRCU for sleeping readers and kfree_rcu for reference-less ones. The changes were tested with various configurations and tools, including KASAN, PROVE_LOCKING, and DEBUG_OBJECTS_RCU_HEAD.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] mm/mempolicy: stop copying the nodemask in the interleave paths
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the unnecessary copying of a nodemask in interleave node selectors, which reduces memory usage and improves performance. The original copy was done to ensure consistency between the node count and the walk, but this is no longer necessary as bounds checking can be used instead. If an empty nodelist or weight is detected, the patch falls back to using numa_node_id(). This change affects several functions in the mm/mempolicy.c file, including weighted_interleave_nid() and interleave_nid(), which are used for allocating pages under a specific memory policy.

review_comments.author: Rakie Kim
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer pointed out that the patch's removal of read_once_policy_nodemask() may cause a potential issue in alloc_pages_bulk_weighted_interleave(), where the function derives per-node counts from a weight total summed over the mask, and a changing mask can make them exceed the request.

Reviewer Rakie Kim agreed that resolving the sleeping-allocation problem using SRCU is a better approach than patching the allocation site and removing copies from the fault path.

Reviewer Rakie Kim noted that after removing the nodemask copy, the loop bound in alloc_pages_bulk_weighted_interleave() no longer matches the actual mask being walked, which can cause the walk to stop short of the intended pages. They suggested counting nodes in the loop that sums weights, as done in weighted_interleave_nid(), to fix this issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello Gregory,

Thanks for the series.

On Fri, 28 Aug 2026 21:59:43 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

---

I went through both patches. Resolving the sleeping-allocation
problem with SRCU rather than patching the allocation site, and
removing the copies from the fault path along the way, looks like
the right direction to me.

---

I have a minor comment on this part. After this change, everything
else reads pol->nodes fresh at the point of use - the weight sum
and the walk both look at the current mask. Only nnodes is still
the count from this earlier read. If the mask changes in between,
the loop bound no longer matches the mask the loop is actually
walking, so the walk can stop short of the pages the weight total
planned for. Would it be better to count the nodes in the loop
that sums the weights, the way weighted_interleave_nid() does it
in this patch?

	nnodes = 0;
	for_each_node_mask(node, pol->nodes) {
		weight_total += table ? table[node] : 1;
		nnodes++;
	}

[...snip...]

Thanks again for your time.

Rakie Kim

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] fs: stamp the current time for a stale delegated ctime update
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the way delegated ctime updates are handled for NFS clients. When a client moves the timestamp backwards on purpose, as utimensat() does, the current time is stamped instead of skipping the update. This ensures that the delegated change remains visible in the ctime. The patch modifies the inode_set_ctime_deleg function to compare the updated timestamp with the existing one after clamping and truncating it, and if they are equal or the update is older, it returns the current time. This prevents a race condition where concurrent updates to the inode can cause the update to be skipped.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] nfsd: accept a backdated timestamp from a delegation holder
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows an NFS client holding a delegation to report backdated file timestamps, which are then accepted by the server without being clamped to the current time. This change is necessary because the client can apply explicit utimensat() calls while holding the delegation, and the server should trust the client's authority over these times. The patch also includes several additional changes to handle cases where the client reports unchanged timestamps or attempts to set a future timestamp.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] nfsd: compare CB_GETATTR times against the inode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NFS server's delegation handling to compare client-reported timestamps against the actual inode times, rather than stale values. This change prevents clients from moving the inode's timestamp backwards by updating it after a previous setattr operation. The patch also removes unnecessary fields from the delegation structure and fixes a bug where an uninitialized struct kstat was being read.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch set allows the NFS server to accept backdated timestamps from a delegation holder, resolving an issue where applications that write files and then update their timestamps (e.g., tar -x, cp -p) cannot properly set these timestamps due to strict attribute delegation rules. The solution involves modifying how the change time is handled on the server side, rather than requiring changes on the client side. This approach aims to improve performance in common use cases while still enforcing necessary security and consistency requirements.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 1/2] fuse: don't shorten the folio descriptor at LLONG_MAX
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) kernel module where the folio descriptor length is shortened when handling reads that exceed LLONG_MAX. This was causing issues with virtio-fs and iomap, leading to incorrect reporting of read bytes pending and leaving unrequested data in the folio. The patch leaves the descriptor length untouched, allowing the reply to be one byte shorter than expected, which is then zeroed out by fuse_copy_folios(). This fix also addresses a bug that existed before the introduction of iomap changes to FUSE.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 2/2] fuse: zero the correct range on a short read reply
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) kernel module where, when a read reply is shorter than requested, it incorrectly zeroes out blocks outside the copied range that are up-to-date or dirty but not yet written back. The patch moves the zeroing logic into the fuse_copy_folios function and only clears the tail of the requested range that was not sent by the server. This ensures that only the correct range is cleared, preventing potential data loss.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes two iomap bugs reported by Sashiko in the FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) kernel module. The first bug occurs when a folio descriptor is shortened at LLONG_MAX, and the second bug incorrectly zeros the wrong range on a short read reply. The patches address these issues to ensure correct behavior and prevent potential data corruption.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v3] mm/memcontrol: skip non-hierarchical memcg-wide stats when v1 is unavailable

version_history.subject: [PATCH v3] mm/memcontrol: skip non-hierarchical memcg-wide stats when v1 is unavailable

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the Linux kernel's memory control group (memcg) statistics by skipping non-hierarchical memcg-wide stats when the v1 version is unavailable. This is done by compiling out the non-hierarchical arrays if CONFIG_MEMCG_V1 is not set, and skipping updates on these arrays even if v1 is supported but blocked by a boot parameter. The patch aims to reduce flush costs by avoiding unnecessary read-modify-write operations, resulting in a 4.1% reduction in memcg-wide aggregation time and a 2.2% reduction in overall flush function time.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 2/7] mm/page_counter: report the number of pages charged
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an optional parameter to the page_counter_try_charge function, which returns the number of pages actually charged to the hierarchy when successful. This change is necessary because in some cases, a charge can be successful without growing the hierarchy size. The new parameter is used by only one caller, try_charge_memcg, and is not intended to introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 3/7] mm/page_counter: introduce per-page_counter stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-page_counter stock to improve the performance of memcg charge and limit checks. The current implementation uses per-cpu stocks, which can lead to expensive hierarchy walks and inefficient cache management. By pushing stock caches down to the page_counter level, each counter is responsible for its own charge, reducing the need for CPU-wide draining and improving scalability when adding new page_counters to a memcg.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 4/7] mm/page_counter: use stock in page_counter_try_charge
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge function to attempt to service a charge request from its stock before attempting to fulfill it through the hierarchy. The patch preserves the existing semantics of stock management, including limiting checks and greedy attempts to refill the stock. It also adds a new function, page_counter_refill_stock, which is used by page_counter_try_charge to refill the stock. No functional changes are intended as no page counters currently enable stock and counter->batch remains at 0.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 5/7] mm/page_counter: introduce an asynchronous drainer
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces an asynchronous drainer for page counters, which iterates through each CPU and flushes any existing charges without affecting unrelated memory cgroups' stock. This approach coalesces duplicate drain requests and improves performance by avoiding unnecessary work on remote CPUs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 6/7] mm/memcontrol: convert memcg to use page_counter_stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch converts the memory cgroup (memcg) to use page_counter_stock, which transparently handles stock usage and refills. This change eliminates a special case in try_charge_memcg and removes the 7-memcg cap, allowing each CPU to cache an unbounded number of pages. The patch also enables draining stock on isolated CPUs and addresses a user-visible change for legacy cgroup v1 (memsw). Unused memcg code is removed, preserving obj_stock and FLUSHING_CACHED_CHARGE.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 7/7] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page_counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series overhauls the memcg (memory cgroup) stock handling, folding the memcg stock into the page_counter level and introducing a new page_counter_stock for memsw to benefit from caching charges. The changes aim to reduce the memsw skew introduced by previous patches, ensuring that memory and memsw charging are synchronized in batches.

Hi Michal! Thanks for taking a look at the series.

> The change of do_memsw_account() is because of re-attaching the memory
> controller between v1 and v2 trees. That's not so common operation (but
> not ruled out), pre-condition for that is that there's only a single
> online memcg, namely the root memcg. So it needs treatment especially at
> memcg offlining (which is what drain_all_stock() (also) does).

Wow, that's good to know. To be completely honest I dont have much
experience with cgroup v1. I didn't realize it wasn't a "switch whenever
you want" type of operation. Good to know that there is some more
guarding there.

> I don't know how expensive page_counter_drain_stock_async() is going to
> be [1] but the v1 parts here could could be guarded with
> !cgroup_on_dfl(memcg->css.cgroup).

The function itself should be pretty quick. It just frees one CPU's
stock, but the rest is just scheduling a job item.

> Regards,
> Michal
> 
> [1] Now, I see in 5/7 that there's the counter->stock check which should
>     be quick bailout on v2 (maybe quicker than the cgroup_on_dfl()
>     Iproposed above).

I'm not entirely sure, it's probably similar : -)
I think they should achieve the same goal, and hopefully it wasn't too
difficult to understand why we don't have the cgroup_on_dfl() there.

Hopefully the rest of the code looks good to you too. Thanks again for
taking a look Michal, I hope you have a great day!
Joshua

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the per-cpu 'stock' from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing for more efficient and independent stock management. The stock is now a property of each counter rather than the CPU, eliminating the need for cross-memcg interference and random victim eviction. This change also enables transparent charging and refilling of stock through page_counter_try_charge(). As a result, multiple sources of stock management can be added to mem_cgroup without tightly coupling them to struct mem_cgroup.
